title: §06-002: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify
description: Multiple-choice practice questions and deep runtime verification for §06-002 (Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify).

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Execution Context Call Stack
cards.question: When a JavaScript function is invoked, what is the exact lifecycle of its Execution Context in the V8 engine?

options.text: It is allocated on the C++ heap and remains until garbage collected by Mark-Sweep.
It is pushed onto the Call Stack, creating Variable and Lexical Environments, and popped off upon function return.
It is queued into the libuv event loop check phase before bytecode evaluation.
It is compiled directly into machine code bypass frames without environment record allocation.

cards.explanation: V8 pushes a new Execution Context onto the Call Stack on function invocation. It initializes LexicalEnvironment and VariableEnvironment records for identifier resolution. When execution finishes, the frame is popped off the Call Stack.
cards.pitfall: Excessive deep recursive function calls without tail call optimization exceed maximum Call Stack size, throwing 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded'.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §9.4 / MDN Web Docs: Call Stack

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: V8 Ignition Bytecode Compilation
cards.question: What is the primary role of Ignition in Google's V8 JavaScript runtime engine?

options.text: A generational garbage collector that compacts young generation semi-spaces.
A fast, memory-efficient bytecode interpreter that generates bytecode from the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST).
An optimizing compiler that compiles hot loops into unboxed assembly via TurboFan.
A cross-platform event loop driver managing async I/O file descriptors.

cards.explanation: V8's Ignition interpreter generates bytecode from ASTs and executes it directly with low memory overhead. Hot code paths profiling feedback are then passed to TurboFan for speculative JIT compilation.
cards.codeSnippet:
$ node --print-bytecode --print-bytecode-filter=calculate app.js
[generated bytecode for function: calculate]
Parameter count 2
Register count 3
LdaNamedProperty a0, [0], [0]
Star r0
Return
cards.pitfall: Writing polymorphic or megamorphic functions with fluctuating hidden classes (shapes) forces TurboFan deoptimization back to Ignition bytecode interpretation.
cards.citation: V8 JavaScript Engine Documentation: Ignition Interpreter Architecture

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Primitive Value Immutability
cards.question: In JavaScript, how are primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, symbol, null, undefined) represented in memory?

options.text: As mutable heap objects whose properties can be reassigned dynamically.
As immutable values where operations return fresh values rather than mutating the original.
As shared pointers that synchronize across Worker threads automatically.
As boxed instances of global prototypes initialized at boot time.

cards.explanation: All primitives in JavaScript are immutable. You cannot alter properties on a primitive; method calls like str.toUpperCase() return brand new strings without altering str in place.
cards.codeSnippet:
let greeting = 'hello';
greeting[0] = 'H'; // Silently fails in sloppy mode; TypeError in strict mode
console.log(greeting); // 'hello'
const upper = greeting.toUpperCase(); // returns new string 'HELLO'
cards.pitfall: Attempting to assign properties to primitives silently creates temporary boxed wrapper objects that are immediately discarded.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §6.1 / MDN Web Docs: Primitive Values

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
cards.question: What causes a `ReferenceError` when accessing a `let` or `const` identifier before its syntactic declaration?

options.text: The identifier is not hoisted into the declarative environment record during compilation.
The identifier is hoisted and bound to the environment record, but remains uninitialized in the TDZ until the declaration statement is evaluated.
The identifier is automatically assigned `undefined` which prohibits read operations.
Strict mode enforces runtime deletion of identifiers declared in block scope.

cards.explanation: Both `let` and `const` variables are hoisted to the beginning of their containing block, but they enter the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Any read or write access before the line where the variable is declared triggers a ReferenceError.
cards.pitfall: Using typeof on a TDZ variable does not safely return 'undefined'; it throws ReferenceError unlike genuinely undeclared variables.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §14.3.1 / You Don't Know JS: Scope & Closures

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Closure Memory Retention
cards.question: How does a closure preserve outer lexical scope bindings, and how can it cause accidental memory leaks in long-running Node.js processes?

options.text: Closures clone the entire process memory space to worker threads.
Inner functions retain a hidden [[Scopes]] reference to their parent LexicalEnvironment, preventing large referenced objects from being garbage collected.
Closures serialize their scope into JSON buffers in the V8 code cache.
Every closure permanently registers an active handle in the libuv threadpool.

cards.explanation: A closure holds an active reference to its parent LexicalEnvironment record via the internal [[Scopes]] chain. Even if the outer function completes, any objects referenced by that LexicalEnvironment cannot be reclaimed by the V8 garbage collector.
cards.pitfall: Unintentionally capturing heavy buffers or database connections in event listeners or interval callbacks prevents GC reclamation and causes steady heap growth.
cards.citation: Node.js Memory Leak Diagnostic Guide / V8 Garbage Collection Mechanics

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Prototypal Inheritance & Prototype Chain
cards.question: When evaluating `obj.property`, what sequence does the JavaScript runtime follow across the prototype chain?

options.text: It queries the constructor function's static properties, then checks the global scope.
It checks own enumerable properties on `obj`, then traverses `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` upward until finding the property or reaching `null`.
It queries `Object.prototype` first, and if found, cascades down to the instance.
It invokes the property getter method on every registered subclass simultaneously.

cards.explanation: Property lookup first inspects the receiver's own property descriptor table. If not found, it steps to its internal [[Prototype]] link (Object.getPrototypeOf), repeating until the property is found or [[Prototype]] terminates at null.
cards.pitfall: Modifying Object.prototype directly alters every object in the JavaScript realm, introducing security risks (prototype pollution) and performance deoptimizations.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §10.1.8 / MDN Web Docs: Inheritance and prototype chain

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Strict Equality vs Abstract Equality
cards.question: What is the key difference between strict equality (`===`) and abstract equality (`==`) according to ECMA-262?

options.text: `===` coerces both operands to strings before comparison, while `==` compares raw pointers.
`===` performs type checking first and returns false if types differ; `==` applies the Abstract Equality Comparison Algorithm to perform implicit coercion.
`===` only works for object references, whereas `==` works for primitive types.
`==` throws a TypeError if compared operands have dissimilar data types.

cards.explanation: The `===` operator compares values without coercion: if Type(x) !== Type(y), it returns false immediately. The `==` operator triggers multi-step coercion rules (e.g. converting booleans and strings to numbers).
cards.codeSnippet:
console.log(0 == ''); // true ('' coerced to 0)
console.log(0 === ''); // false (number !== string)
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false
cards.pitfall: Relying on abstract equality (`==`) with truthy/falsy checks leads to unexpected bugs with empty strings, 0, false, and empty arrays.
cards.citation: ECMAScript 2024 Specification §7.2.14 / You Don't Know JS: Types & Grammar

cards.concept: Promises: Resolving, Rejecting & Promisify: Macro-tasks vs Micro-tasks Execution
cards.question: When a script resolves a Promise and schedules `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, what is the guaranteed execution order in the event loop?

options.text: `setTimeout` callback runs first because it is registered in the host timer queue.
Micro-task queue (Promise.then callbacks) drains completely immediately after the current call stack clears, before any macro-task (timer) runs.
Both run concurrently in separate threads inside libuv's threadpool.
The event loop randomly alternates between micro-tasks and macro-tasks based on scheduling priority.

cards.explanation: Micro-tasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, process.nextTick in Node.js) drain completely before the event loop advances to the next macro-task phase (such as timer callbacks from setTimeout/setInterval).
cards.pitfall: Starving the event loop: recursively enqueuing micro-tasks (e.g. endless process.nextTick) prevents the event loop from ever reaching I/O or timer phases.
cards.citation: Node.js Event Loop, Timers, and process.nextTick() Official Guide
